topic.subject: social
topic.title: From trade to territory: the East India Company
topic.scope: Battle of Plassey, Buxar, diwani, subsidiary alliance, doctrine of lapse, Tipu Sultan

concepts.name: Transition from Trading Company to Political Power

misconceptions.statement: The East India Company arrived in India with the primary goal of ruling the country.
misconceptions.why: Students project modern political knowledge onto the past, assuming the British had a grand master plan from the start.
misconceptions.fix: The Company initially came only for trade and profit; political power was acquired gradually to protect their commercial interests.

probe.question: Why did the East India Company first set up factories in India?
probe.wrong_answer: To establish a government and rule over the Indian people.

concepts.name: Military Conflicts and Acquisition of Diwani Rights

misconceptions.statement: The Battle of Plassey was a massive, evenly matched war between two great armies.
misconceptions.why: Textbooks often emphasize the 'Battle' aspect, leading students to imagine a large-scale conventional war rather than a conspiracy.
misconceptions.fix: Plassey was largely won through the betrayal of Mir Jafar, as Siraj-ud-Daulah's forces did not fight effectively.

probe.question: Why did the British win the Battle of Plassey easily?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the British army was much larger and stronger than the Nawab's army.

misconceptions.statement: Diwani rights meant the British became the kings of India.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the administrative right to collect revenue with the total sovereign power of a monarch.
misconceptions.fix: Diwani rights only allowed the Company to collect land revenue, while the Nawab still held formal administrative and judicial responsibilities.

probe.question: What did the grant of Diwani mean for the Company?
probe.wrong_answer: It meant the Company became the new King and could make all laws for the people.

concepts.name: Subsidiary Alliance and Doctrine of Lapse

misconceptions.statement: The Doctrine of Lapse was a law that forced all Indian rulers to give up their kingdoms.
misconceptions.why: Students overgeneralize the policy, failing to distinguish between kingdoms with natural heirs and those without.
misconceptions.fix: The policy only applied to kingdoms where the ruler died without a natural male heir, preventing the adoption of an heir to the throne.

probe.question: Could a king with a natural son lose his kingdom under the Doctrine of Lapse?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the British could take over any kingdom they wanted using this law.
